translationRepairs: Jingzhen said: "De he who launched the cause with utmost sincerity; Liusheng killed him on his own authority—if not executed, there can be no government.

德其 is the personal name Deji; the existing literal text splits it into an English word and pronoun.

Fortuitously today Heaven guides our hearts; you and others lower your hearts—we shall greatly restore Liang's line, trusting in fortune from the former emperor; how dare I not muster warriors to follow you!"

Today, by good fortune, Heaven guides our hearts; you and the others humble yourselves—we shall greatly restore Liang's line, trusting in fortune from the former emperor; how dare I not muster warriors to follow you!"
The proposal improves the awkward opening and 降心, but 'by good fortune' reads more naturally while preserving the uncertain opening of the received text.

In martial force he was wanting, yet in rhetoric he was ample. Men who steal the names of benevolence and righteousness to mislead the age and stir custom are precisely those the sages condemn without mercy.

As for Xian, he was wanting in martial force but ample in rhetoric. Men who steal the names of benevolence and righteousness to mislead the age and corrupt custom are precisely those the sages must punish.
觀銑 names Xian as the subject; the revision restores that referent while keeping the judgment idiomatic.

The chapter's other notices and the received biography identify Li Xiaogong as Prince of Zhao Commandery; 越 in this sentence is a source-text error. The offices are also restored without treating place names as personal titles.
